interactive.title: The family gallery
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on five graph shapes. A gallery has five tabs, the line, the square, the cube, the one-over and the square root, each with its plain rule and a law from work written under it. Drag the x marker along the bottom axis and a point rides the curve, with its x and y read out and each pair added as a row of a small table. On the line, y = x, drawn from −3 to 3, each equal step across gives the same rise, and doubling an input doubles its output. On the square, y = x², drawn from −3 to 3, a negative input gives the same output as the positive one, so the curve is a U, and its outputs 0, 1, 4, 9 rise by 1, 3 and 5. Its law is the power lost in a cable run, P = I²R, with the run's resistance taken as 1 Ω, where a negative current means the same current flowing the other way. On the cube, y = x³, drawn from −2 to 2, 1 gives 1 and 2 gives 8, and a negative input gives a negative output, so the curve is an S through 0. Its law is the propeller law, a model that breaks down at partial load, and its puzzle uses a fan, whose power also goes with the cube of its speed, with speed and power as fractions of full. On the one-over, y = 1/x, drawn from −4 to 4, the point runs off up the side as x nears 0 from the right and down the side from the left, and there is no point at 0, and negative inputs make a second curve in the bottom left. Its law is Ohm's law on a 12 V supply, I = 12/R. On the square root, y = √x, drawn from 0 to 9, the curve starts at 0 and has nothing to its left, and its outputs 1, 2, 3 need inputs 1, 4 and 9. Its law is flow from a pressure difference, both as fractions of full. One screen adds a level line you drag up and down: on the square it cuts twice anywhere above the bottom of the U, which is called many-to-one, and on the other four at most once. The tab row is hidden on the table and gas puzzles. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick shows the slip that makes it. The second puzzle picks which of three tables comes from a line. The last two mix the families: which currents lose 9 W in the 1 Ω run, and which shape a gas's pressure against its volume makes, at a fixed temperature, when halving the volume doubles the pressure.
interactive.ignores: The laws are drawn as their plain rules. A real cable's resistance changes a little as it warms, and the propeller law is a model that works well in steady high-speed running but breaks down at partial load, such as at a slower speed. The 1 Ω run and the 12 V supply are example values. Each graph shows only part of its curve: the square, cube and root carry on climbing past the edge of the picture, and the one-over keeps getting closer to the axes without touching them.

explain.text:
Five graph shapes turn up again and again: the line, the square, the cube, the one-over and the square root. Each is a family with a tell-tale look, and each is the shape of a law you use at work. Each shape comes from its rule, and the quickest way to see why is to double the input and watch the output.

On the line, y = x, every equal step across gives the same rise, so it is straight. The transmitter from the last lesson is a line, a straight-line rule of the kind instruments use.[^2] On the square, y = x², double the input and the output goes up four times, because 2 × 2 = 4. Its outputs 0, 1, 4, 9 rise by 1, then 3, then 5, so the curve climbs faster and faster. A negative input gives the same output as the positive one, because a minus times a minus is a plus, so the left half mirrors the right and the curve is a U, called a [[parabola]]. Power lost in a cable depends on the square of the current,[^3] P = I²R. On a 1 Ω run, 3 A loses 9 W and 6 A loses 36 W, not the 18 W a line would give. On the cube, y = x³, double the input and the output goes up eight times, because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. A negative input now gives a negative output, so the curve comes up from the bottom left, flattens through 0, where small inputs cubed are tiny, and climbs to the top right. A ship's engine load goes with the cube of the propeller's speed,[^4] a model that works well in steady high-speed running but breaks down at partial load, such as at a slower speed.[^9] A fan's power goes with the cube of its speed too, so at half speed it uses 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125 of full power, one eighth, which is 12.5%.[^8]

On the one-over, y = 1/x, double the input and the output halves, because 1 shared by twice as much is half as much. Ohm's law on a fixed voltage is one: on 12 V, 3 Ω draws 4 A and 6 Ω draws 2 A. As the input shrinks towards 0 the output grows past any number you name, and dividing by 0 has no answer, so the curve never touches the up axis and has no point at 0. Negative inputs give a matching curve in the bottom left, so the graph comes in two pieces. A gas at a fixed temperature does the same, as you met in Proportional reasoning: halve its volume and its pressure doubles. Plot its pressure against its volume and you get this shape, called a [[hyperbola]].[^5] On the square root, y = √x, it takes four times the input to double the output, because √4 = 2. Its outputs 1, 2, 3 need inputs 1, 4, 9, gaps that keep growing, so the curve starts at 0, rises steeply and then flattens. It has nothing to the left of 0, which lesson 4 explains. A flow meter's pressure difference goes with the square of the flow, so the flow is found from the square root of the pressure difference.[^6] The root of a number between 0 and 1 is bigger than the number: √0.5 = 0.707, so a 12 mA signal from the cell is 50% of the pressure difference but 71% of the flow.[^1]

The families also differ in what a level line does. On the square, a level line above the bottom cuts the U twice, so two different inputs give the same output and it is many-to-one.[^7] On a sloping line, the cube, the one-over and the square root, a level line cuts at most once, so each output comes from one input only, and the function is called [[one-to-one]]. So a function's graph need not be a line or a U. The S, the two-piece curve and the curve that starts at 0 are functions too, because each input they take gives one output.

**Five shapes, the line, the square's U, the cube's S, the one-over's two curves and the root that starts at 0, each come from what the rule does to a doubled input, to a negative input and to 0, and each is the shape of a working law.**

analogy.text: Think of the waveforms on a scope. Once you know a sine, a square wave and a sawtooth by sight, the shape on the screen gives you a strong first clue about what is driving the circuit, before you measure a thing. The five families are the same kind of reference set for laws: the shape of a graph tells you which rule is likely behind it, and a table of readings confirms it.
analogy.breaks: A scope draws a signal against time, and its shapes repeat. These graphs are an output against any input, and these five never repeat. A family can also be slid or stretched (lessons 5 and 6), so you look for the tell-tale features rather than the exact size.

practice.text:
- Make a short table: put in 1, 2 and 4, and a negative or two if the inputs can be negative.
- See what each doubling does to the output.
- Look for the tell-tale shape: straight, a U, an S, two curves hugging the axes, or a curve starting at 0.
- Name the family, then check one more input against its rule.

**Rule of thumb:** On the plain rules, doubling the input doubles the output on the line through 0, makes it four times on the square and eight times on the cube, and halves it on the one-over. On the root it takes four times the input to double the output.

**Worked example:** A 12 V supply through 2 Ω draws 6 A, through 4 Ω draws 3 A and through 8 Ω draws 1.5 A. Each doubling of the resistance halves the current, so this is the one-over family, I = 12/R. Check: 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5.

**Common mistakes**
- Treating every law as a line. Doubling the current makes the cable loss four times, not twice.
- Forgetting the negative input on the square. 9 comes from −3 as well as 3.
- Mixing up the square and the cube because both bend. Try a negative input: the square gives a positive output, the cube a negative one.
- Reading a value at 0 off the one-over. It has no point there.
